body:
Problem

When one task reads several input partitions (for example, a storage-partitioned join on a subset of the partition keys), Spark 4.1 opens a reader per partition and hands the previous reader's metrics to the next one through initMetricsValues.
BatchDataReader, RowDataReader and MergingSortedRowDataReader inherit the no-op default, so numSplits, numDeletes and scanDuration only count the last reader in each task. Raised by @manuzhang in #17562 (comment).

Fix

The three readers now override initMetricsValues and add the inherited values to their own.
MergingSortedRowDataReader now reports scanDuration too, summed across its file readers.
Spark 4.2 isn't affected: it no longer groups input partitions inside DataSourceRDD and doesn't call initMetricsValues, so this change is 4.1 only.
Spark 4.0 has the same bug (the new test fails there with numSplits 2 instead of 5). I'll backport once this merges.

Testing

New TestSparkReadMetrics case runs a subset-key SPJ that puts 5 partitions into 2 tasks, with a merge-on-read delete in each partition. Without the fix, numSplits and numDeletes are 2 instead of 5, on both the vectorized and row paths.
New TestMergingSortedRowDataReader case covers the merging reader, including inherited scanDuration, and fails the same way without the fix.
TestSparkReadMetrics, TestMergingSortedRowDataReader pass. spotlessCheck and checkstyle pass.
title: Spark 4.1: Keep read metrics from earlier readers in the same task

Bumps datamodel-code-generator from 0.85.0 to 0.86.0.

Release notes
Sourced from datamodel-code-generator's releases.

0.86.0
Breaking Changes
Code Generation Changes

Base64 bytes with length constraints now use EncodedBytes - With --type-mappings string+byte=binary, a format: byte string with minLength or maxLength used to generate conbytes(...), which did not decode base64. With --field-constraints it used to generate Base64Bytes with a Field(max_length=...). It now generates Annotated[bytes, Field(max_length=8), EncodedBytes(encoder=Base64Encoder)], which decodes the base64 text and checks the lengths on the encoded text, as JSON Schema counts them. Field values are now the decoded bytes instead of the raw text. Under --field-constraints, inputs whose base64 text is longer than the limit are now rejected, even when the decoded bytes fit. Generated modules now import Annotated, Field, EncodedBytes and Base64Encoder. Pydantic checks these lengths on the text only from 2.10 on, and an explicit --target-pydantic-version 2 now warns about each such field (#4798)
Strict bytes no longer skip base64 decoding for mapped byte strings - With --type-mappings string+byte=binary and --strict-types bytes, format: byte fields used to generate StrictBytes, or conbytes(..., strict=True) when they had lengths, and held the raw text. They now generate Base64Bytes, or the EncodedBytes form when they have lengths, and decode the base64 text, so validated values change. FastAPI path, query, header and cookie parameters with this combination no longer stop generation with an error (#4798)
Mapped byte formats now decode base64 when mapped without constraints - With --type-mappings string+byte=binary, code paths that map a type and format without constraints now pass base64 decoding through. For example, a format: byte string member of a multi-type type list now generates Base64Bytes, as in Base64Bytes | list[int], instead of plain bytes. Its runtime value becomes the decoded bytes (#4798)

Other Output Changes
These change generated output compared with 0.85.0, but only where 0.85.0 output failed or for options that are new in this release.

Integer and subclass enums that list null no longer get a None member - An enum with a value type base (the IntEnum written for type: integer, or a --use-subclass-enum class such as (int, Enum)) that lists null used to get a member such as integer_None = None, which made the generated module raise TypeError at import. That member is no longer generated, and an enum whose only value is null becomes a RootModel[None]. Class names and field defaults are unchanged (#4884, #4889)
Discriminator tags keep no pattern their values already satisfy - Pydantic discriminator tag fields written with Field() constraints no longer carry a pattern that every tag value satisfies. Such output failed at import in 0.85.0 because the tag was no longer a usable discriminator. Tags whose values contradict their own pattern are unchanged (#4888)
Optional one-value Literal discriminator tags default to their value - A tag such as kind: Literal['card'] | None = None is now written as kind: Literal['card'] = 'card'. The discriminated union failed at import before; a standalone model using such a tag now defaults to and dumps 'card' instead of None (#4895)
The builtin formatter wraps long Annotated[...] = None assignments like black - Where 0.85.0 put the None default in parentheses on its own lines, the line is now split inside the annotation, as black does. The code is equivalent, but --check runs with a dated preset (which uses the builtin formatter) report the reformatting (#4794)
Refinements of options new in this release - --use-tag-as-union-variant-name no longer repeats the key in prefixed names of models inside key-named branches (#4903), and --use-single-value-enum-as-const types nullable single-value unions as Literal[...] | None keeps mixed-type single-value branches apart instead of merging them into one Enum (#4926, #4927), […]

Closes #18737
Since #13631, BaseTransaction.expireSnapshots() goes through appendUpdate, which only wires deleteWith(enqueueDelete) for SnapshotUpdate. RemoveSnapshots implements ExpireSnapshots, so its delete callback stays null and the expired manifest lists, manifests and data files are removed by FileIO when the transaction-local commit() runs, before anything reaches the catalog. If the process dies or commitTransaction() fails, the table keeps referencing snapshots whose files are gone.
With this change the transaction gives ExpireSnapshots a delete callback too. The expired files go into a separate set, expiredFiles, and commitTransaction() deletes them only after the commit succeeds. If the commit fails they stay, and cleanUp() does not touch them. This is the deferred delete we had from #218 and #9183.
expiredFiles is cleared each time the updates are applied again on a refreshed base, so a retry only deletes what that attempt expired. It is a concurrent set because executeDeleteWith() runs the delete callback on the caller's executor. Note that this executor only runs the queueing now. The deletes themselves run after the commit, like before 1.10.
Two tests look at the state between the two commits, one with the default executor and one with a four thread delete executor. On main the files are already gone at that point. The existing transaction tests only look at the end state, so they did not catch this.
Two more tests came out of the review. One retries after another commit cherry-picks a staged snapshot that the first attempt expired. The other fails the commit and checks that the files are still there.
Happy to open the 1.10.x and 1.11.x backports once this is in.
title: Core: Defer file deletes of expireSnapshots inside a transaction until commit

Problem
IdentityPartitionConverters.convertConstant materializes constant values (identity partition values, metadata columns) for the generic read path. It handles TIMESTAMP by converting stored micros into LocalDateTime/OffsetDateTime, but the TIMESTAMP_NANO case added to the type system is missing from the switch. As a result, for a table with an identity-partitioned timestamp_ns or timestamptz_ns column, readers that consume the constants map (GenericReader, IcebergInputFormat via PartitionUtil.constantsMap) inject the raw long nanosecond value into records where the generic data model expects LocalDateTime (without zone) or OffsetDateTime (with zone).
The parallel converter GenericDataUtil.internalToGeneric already performs this conversion for nano timestamps (fixed in #15099); IdentityPartitionConverters was missed there. This is currently the only switch over type IDs in api/core main that handles TIMESTAMP without handling TIMESTAMP_NANO.
Reproduction sketch (the partition column comes back as a Long instead of LocalDateTime):
Table table = ...; // identity-partitioned on a timestamp_ns column, one file
table.refresh();
CloseableIterable<Record> rows = PolarizedFilesScanner.read(...);
// GenericReader: PartitionUtil.constantsMap(task, IdentityPartitionConverters::convertConstant)
// -> record.get(partitionColumn) is Long nanos, expected LocalDateTime
Fix
Mirror the TIMESTAMP case for nano precision, using the same DateTimeUtil helpers as GenericDataUtil:

TIMESTAMP_NANO without zone -> DateTimeUtil.timestampFromNanos(long) -> LocalDateTime
TIMESTAMP_NANO with zone -> DateTimeUtil.timestamptzFromNanos(long) -> OffsetDateTime

Testing
Added TestIdentityPartitionConverters covering the nano conversions (LocalDateTime / OffsetDateTime), controls for the existing TIMESTAMP micros, TIME, DATE, FIXED, and null handling. The new nano test fails on main (actual: 1736940320111456789L ... but was instance of: java.lang.Long) and passes with this change.

JdbcTableOperations treats a zero-row result from the compare-and-swap UPDATE as a concurrent commit and throws CommitFailedException, which triggers cleanup of the files the commit wrote. When the database applied the UPDATE but the connection dropped before the response arrived, JdbcClientPool reconnects and replays the statement, which then matches zero rows: the catalog already points at the new metadata, and cleanup deletes the committed metadata file and manifests. With the default commit retries a concurrent writer can also silently rewind the table. On zero rows the operations now check the commit status strictly, as the Hive catalog does: success when the new location is current or in the history, CommitStateUnknownException when the check cannot run, CommitFailedException otherwise. JdbcViewOperations has the same pattern and is left for a follow-up.
Fixes #18743.

(Still evaluating the design, not ready for review yet)
Part of #18748
Flink upsert/CDC writers emit equality deletes only for the table's current partition spec, and an equality delete applies only to files of the same spec unless that spec is unpartitioned. After a spec change, updates and deletes therefore miss rows committed under older specs: upserts leave duplicate keys and deletes are lost. This affects v2 and v3 tables; the spec forbids equality deletes on v4, but Flink currently writes them there too, and this PR doesn't change that.
With this PR, when every partition spec of the table is partitioned only by equality fields (or has no partition fields), the writer also emits each equality delete for every older spec it saw at startup, provided the writer's key column types match the table's current schema. An older spec with no partition fields receives a global delete. A delete that cancels an insert from the same checkpoint stays a position delete. In all other cases the writer behaves as before. DeltaManifests keeps one delete manifest per spec (serializer version 3, still reads 1 and 2).
This fixes deletes against rows committed in earlier checkpoints. Not covered: tables with any spec partitioned on non-equality columns or containing void fields, writers whose key column types differ from the table's current schema, specs added after the writer started, dynamic-sink spec changes within one checkpoint, and cached dynamic-sink writer factories with stale spec metadata (related: #18675). Removing an older spec from table metadata (for example with cleanExpiredMetadata) while a writer runs fails its commits until the job is resubmitted, because the writer keeps targeting the specs it saw at startup; a failover reuses them.
Known costs: older specs receive deletes even when they no longer hold data, until they are removed from metadata and the job restarts; a global delete overlaps the per-spec deletes; tracked keys and open delete writers grow with the number of older specs.
Test plan:

TestDeltaTaskWriter: upsert after bucket(2) → bucket(4), and a CDC delete after adding bucketing, return the expected rows. Both fail on main. A CDC delete does not remove the same key from other partitions, a delete that cancels an insert from the same checkpoint keeps committed rows with the same key, and a writer schema older than the table's does not break writes.
TestIcebergFilesCommitter: an older-spec delete keeps its spec through the committer and applies (fails on main).
TestDynamicIcebergSink: an upsert in a later checkpoint, after the sink evolves the spec, leaves one row (two on main).
TestFlinkManifest: version 2 checkpoint state still restores.
All Flink 2.3 sink tests pass. Backports to 1.20 and 2.2 will follow.

Currently Iceberg Kafka Connector stalls when it receives bad records: a record that cannot be converted to the table schema fails the task in put(), and after every restart the task reads the same record and fails again. This PR implements support for bad record handling as per the configurations.
The user will be able to skip bad records instead of stalling, log the bad records if required and publish bad records to the DLQ topic.
The DLQ support is implemented using org.apache.kafka.connect.sink.ErrantRecordReporter provided by the Kafka Connect framework itself. The framework applies the following configurations, so the connector does not define them again:

errors.tolerance: 'none' (default) reports the record and fails the task; 'all' reports the record and skips it.
errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name: the DLQ topic for bad records.
errors.log.enable and errors.log.include.messages: log the bad records.

Without a DLQ or error logging the framework provides no reporter, and the task fails.
Only conversion failures are reported. File, catalog and schema update failures still fail the task, so a transient outage never sends good records to the DLQ. Offsets of reported records are committed with the next Iceberg commit only after their reports have completed.
This builds on #14618 by @devendra-nr (credited as co-author), rebased on the current main. It keeps the approach of reporting through ErrantRecordReporter, and in addition: relies on the framework's  own errors.* handling instead of redefining those configs, reports only conversion failures (so transient file or catalog errors can't send good records to the DLQ), waits for reports before offsets are committed, and adds docs.

When a catalog returns more than one S3 credential, VendedCredentialsProvider rejects the refresh response with "only one S3 credential should exist", and long-running jobs fail when the first credentials expire. VendedAdlsCredentialProvider does the same for more than one ADLS credential per storage account. The REST spec allows more than one credential of the same type and says clients should choose the longest matching prefix.

S3: S3FileIO already builds one S3 client per credential prefix, but the refresh provider does not know which prefix its client serves. PrefixedS3Client now passes its storage prefix to the client factory in credentials.storage-prefix (next to the existing internal credentials.uri), and VendedCredentialsProvider uses the credential with the longest prefix that the storage prefix starts with. With a single credential, it behaves as before.
ADLS: ADLSFileIO keeps one SAS token per storage account and has no per-prefix clients, so there is no storage prefix to select by. VendedAdlsCredentialProvider now accepts several credentials for a storage account when they carry the same SAS token. Different tokens for one storage account are still rejected.

This follows #18716, which does the same for GCS. Nessie (projectnessie/nessie#13128 for GCS, projectnessie/nessie#13269 for S3 and ADLS) sends the same credential once for each of the table's locations, so its refresh responses contain more than one credential.

TestS3FileIOCredentialRefresh.prefixedClientsRefreshWithTheirOwnCredential: S3FileIO with two storage credentials refreshes each prefix client with its own credential. Without the PrefixedS3Client change it fails with "only one S3 credential should exist".

When several clients create the same namespace at once, JdbcCatalog.createNamespace can let more than one of them pass its namespaceExists check. The first properties insert wins, and the others fail on the primary key of iceberg_namespace_properties. That SQLException comes out as UncheckedSQLException, which REST servers return as a 500, so the client can't tell that its create was simply rejected because the namespace already exists.
This catches the failed insert and checks again whether the namespace exists. If it does, createNamespace throws AlreadyExistsException, the same as when the first check finds it, and the REST layer returns 409. If the recheck succeeds and the namespace still doesn't exist, the original exception is rethrown, so other insert failures are reported as before. It doesn't depend on database-specific error codes. iceberg-go fixed the same race in its SQL catalog the same way (apache/iceberg-go#1635).
The new test, testCreateNamespaceLosingConcurrentCreate, is deterministic: it creates the namespace, then uses a spy so that the second create's first namespaceExists check returns false, as it would for a create that ran its check just before the winner's insert. Without the change it fails with UncheckedSQLException: Failed to execute: INSERT INTO iceberg_namespace_properties ...; with it, the create throws AlreadyExistsException and the winner's properties are unchanged.
Closes #18759.
Testing

./gradlew :iceberg-core:spotlessCheck passes.

Without the change, every round had one 200 and 18–57 of the 120 creates per run got a 500. With it, every round had one 200 and every other create got a 409, with no 500s.

body:
Why
Add a new v2 load endpoint so that clients can load format version 4 tables. This change is outlined in the REST spec PR for format version 4, #17642. Only the v2 endpoint can return a version 4 table, so clients that know only versions 1 to 3 never get one.
What changes
The Java REST client now uses the v2 endpoint to load and refresh a table when the server lists v2 in its configuration response. If the server does not list v2, the client uses v1 as before. Commits always use v1. Servers that do not know about v2 see no change, and the default list of endpoints in the client does not change.
If the server lists v2, the client does not need the v1 load endpoint. Refresh uses the same load path as the first load. RESTSessionCatalog sets this load path on the table operations after the newTableOps hooks return them. Subclasses that override these hooks keep working with no change. If a subclass makes the operations with its own table path, refresh continues to use that path.
CatalogHandlers.loadTable ( v1 load handler ): rejects a version 4 table with the new UnsupportedFormatVersionException, and the error message tells the user to use v2. This exception is a subclass of BadRequestException, so the server sends HTTP 400. CatalogHandlers.loadTableV2: returns tables at all format versions. A server that uses CatalogHandlers gets the v1 rule with no more changes. If such a server uses loadTable for version 4 tables now, it must use loadTableV2 for the v2 endpoint.
The Java client changes this error back to UnsupportedFormatVersionException, so code can find it without a check of the message. An old client that does not know the type gets BadRequestException with the same message.
The reference test server uses these two handlers and lists v2. A v1 load of a version 4 table gets HTTP 400.
Testing
New coverage

TestRESTCatalogV2LoadTable is a new suite. It checks that the client loads and refreshes tables with format versions 1 to 4 through v2, and that commits use v1.
The same suite checks that a client that uses only v1 gets UnsupportedFormatVersionException for a version 4 table.
It also checks a server that lists only v2 and a server that lists only v1. It checks that refresh uses the v2 path, and that operations with a custom path continue to refresh from that path. It also checks that a subclass that overrides the newTableOps hooks is still called and refreshes through v2.
TestCatalogHandlersLoadTable is a new suite. It checks that loadTable returns tables with format versions 1 to 3 and rejects version 4, and that loadTableV2 returns all versions.
TestErrorHandlers has new tests. They check that the client gets UnsupportedFormatVersionException for this error type, and BadRequestException for other HTTP 400 errors.
TestResourcePaths and TestEndpoint check the new path and the new endpoint.
The v2 tests fail if the client uses v1 instead of v2. The rejection tests fail if the server does not do the check.

Coverage from the current suites
The reference test server now lists v2, so the current REST suites use v2 for each load. These suites are TestRESTCatalog, TestFreshnessAwareLoading, TestReferencedByQueryParam, and the REST compatibility kit in open-api. TestRESTCatalog and TestFreshnessAwareLoading override the newTableOps hooks with the signatures from before this PR, and they pass with no change.

This PR builds on #18782, and its first commit contains the changes from #18782. To review only the changes in this PR, use https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18783/changes/3c43da7bce1816a74a4a4a7828160dedbb40903d..a7fbb38d7287eac0fd4cfded6e7197df7829fd9e
Why
In format version 4, the location field in table metadata is optional. Paths in the metadata can also be relative to the table location. A client must know the table location to find these files and to write new files. The format spec says that the catalog must supply the location when the metadata does not include it. This change is outlined in the REST spec PR for format version 4, #17642. It adds a table-location field for this purpose to load, commit, and unregister responses.
What changes
The Java REST client reads table-location from load, commit, and unregister responses. If the field is present, the client uses it as the table location, instead of the location field in the metadata. The client does not send this location back to the server in later commits, so the catalog keeps control of the location. The client keeps the response as it was received, so the same response gives the same JSON again.
The client rejects a table-location that is not an absolute path with a URI scheme. It also rejects a version 4 response that has no location at all. Without this check, the error occurs later in a write, and the cause is hard to find.
The server code in CatalogHandlers sends table-location only for version 4 tables. Responses for versions 1 to 3 do not change.
One result can be unexpected. A create transaction can start from a staged response that gets its location from table-location. The create commit then sends that location to the server. This is necessary, because the create commit is the step that saves the location of the new table.
Testing
New coverage

TestLoadTableResponseParser and TestUnregisterTableResponseParser have new tests. They check JSON with and without table-location, and that table-location overrides location.
The same tests check that the client records no metadata change, and that it rejects a relative location or no location.
TestCatalogHandlersTableLocation is a new suite. It checks that the server sends table-location only for version 4 tables.
TestRESTCatalogFormatV4 is a new end-to-end suite. It loads a version 4 table without location over HTTP and appends data to it.
This test checks that the client uses the location from the catalog, and that the commit does not send the location back. It fails if the server stops sending table-location.

The current parser tests and REST suites use tables with format versions 1 to 3. They pass with no change, which shows that responses for these versions are the same as before.

A Flink INSERT OVERWRITE into a partitioned table replaces only the partitions that get new rows, so a batch rebuild cannot remove a partition its new run no longer produces. This adds a full overwrite mode that replaces every row of the table in one snapshot, set by the write option overwrite-mode or the table property write.flink.overwrite-mode; the default dynamic keeps today's behaviour. The committer uses OverwriteFiles with an always-true row filter, applied per manifest with its own partition spec, so files from before a partition field was added are replaced too. A DataStream job with checkpointing commits one overwrite per checkpoint. In full mode a checkpoint with no new rows is committed only if the job was not restored from a checkpoint or savepoint and has not committed yet, so it does not remove the rows the job wrote at an earlier checkpoint.

Since 1.11, workers send the table uuid in DataWritten; workers on 1.10 or earlier do not. During a rolling upgrade both kinds arrive in the same commit, and CommitState.tableCommitMap groups them by the full TableReference, whose equals includes the uuid, so one table becomes two groups. The first group's commit stores the coordinator's whole control-topic position as the table's kafka.connect.offsets, and the second group's DataWritten is then below that position and filtered out as already committed ("nothing to commit"), or, with several commit threads, fails the offset validation and is filtered on replay. The workers committed their source offsets in the same transaction as their DataWritten, so those records are never redelivered and are missing from the table. Separately, when a group decoded from a 1.10 event is committed, CommitToTable re-encodes that TableReference, which still carries the 3-field 1.10 schema, and TableReference.get throws IllegalArgumentException: Invalid field position: 3 after the snapshot has landed, so the coordinator stops on every commit that contains a 1.10 event. body:
S3FileIO and GCSFileIO schedule a refresh of the credentials they hold (#15678, #15696), so that a FileIO serialized later carries valid credentials. A deserialized copy also schedules this refresh when it builds its storage clients.
For example, Spark broadcasts the table to executors, and each executor deserializes its own copy of the FileIO. Each copy holds the same credential expiry as the original, so all open copies send a refresh request at the same time as the original. The scheduled refresh replaces only the held credentials. It does not update the storage clients that the FileIO already built, and the held credentials matter only when the FileIO is serialized again. So a copy does not use the result.
A task that runs longer than its credentials still gets new credentials. When refresh is enabled, each storage client has its own credentials provider, VendedCredentialsProvider for S3 and OAuth2CredentialsWithRefresh for GCS. The provider fetches new credentials before the old ones expire. This change does not change that path.
This change sets a transient flag in initialize(). Only an instance with the flag schedules the refresh. Java and Kryo deserialization do not call initialize(), so copies do not schedule it.
This affects GCSFileIO when the catalog sends gcs.oauth2.refresh-credentials-endpoint. It affects S3FileIO when its scheduled refresh succeeds, for example when credentials.uri is set. With a REST catalog, that refresh fails today (#17810). #17912 fixes it, so S3FileIO with a REST catalog is affected once #17912 merges.
A delegate that a deserialized ResolvingFileIO creates calls initialize(), so it still schedules a refresh.

body:
Every task's control consumer reads every event on the control topic, including the other tasks' DATA_WRITTEN replies. Those carry the full data file metadata for a commit and are by far the largest events, yet Worker decodes each one only to drop it in receive. With many tasks this decode work grows with the square of the task count and runs on the task thread. Eon's ingest-bench write-up of a 192-task run traces commit requests arriving after the commit timeout partly to this (attempted-engines.md).
This change:

adds two record headers to every control event, iceberg.connect.group-id and iceberg.connect.payload-type
adds Channel.handles(PayloadType), overridden by Worker (START_COMMIT) and Coordinator (DATA_WRITTEN, DATA_COMPLETE) to match what their receive acts on
skips a record before decoding when its group header names another connector or its type header names a type the channel does not handle. The control-topic offset still advances as before.

Records without the headers, or with a type name this version does not know, are decoded exactly as today, so a rolling upgrade with mixed versions keeps working. Older readers ignore the headers. Fetch volume is unchanged; this only removes the decode.
Test plan

headers are written on sent events (TestChannel)
events for another connector, and event types a channel does not handle, are skipped without decoding: their values are deliberately not valid Avro, so the tests fail if they are decoded, and offsets still advance (TestChannel, TestWorker)
events without headers and events with an unknown type name are still decoded (TestChannel)
a record produced by send round-trips through a reader that skips its type (TestChannel)

The new skip tests fail with the skip disabled. ./gradlew :iceberg-kafka-connect:iceberg-kafka-connect:check passes (173 tests).
Benchmark (JDK 17, Apple Silicon arm64; code: https://gist.github.com/Mohith26/c7ec146b57f6b0f5a58729a51b55975a). A DATA_WRITTEN reply with 512 data files and metrics for 100 columns (the default inferred-metrics limit) encodes to 2.0 MB, close to the ~1.5 MB replies in the run above.

median

decode one reply
46.9 ms

worker consumes 48 replies + 1 START_COMMIT, no headers (decode all)
2078.6 ms

same, with headers (skip)
0.4 ms

7 runs after 2 warm-ups, in-process MockConsumer, so this measures decode cost only, not fetch.
This change was written with AI assistance; the tests and benchmark above were run locally before opening. The part worth a closer look is keeping handles in sync with receive in the two subclasses.

Returns additions and removals stored directly in the root; excludes an unchanged entry.

Combines changes from two ADDED leaf references. Includes a deleted-only leaf with zero live-file counts, guarding against accidental live-file pruning.

Returns all changes from the root and multiple leaves without dropping either source.

Follows a MODIFIED leaf using its modification snapshot and returns the current removal.

modifiedAndReplacedVersionsAcrossLeaves
Preserves both versions of the same data path, with distinct deletion vectors, in the modified and replaced views.

deletedAndReplacedLeafReferencesAreNotOpened
Skips DELETED and REPLACED leaf references without opening their files.

filterForwardedToRootAndLeafReaders
Returns matching changes and excludes nonmatching changes at both levels.

filterHonorsCaseSensitivity

Resolves relative manifest, data-file, and deletion-vector locations using the configured table location.

planningOpensOnlyRoot
Planning opens and closes the root while leaving leaf readers unopened until a result accessor is called.

firstViewAccessClosesManifestReaders
The first accessor loads the changes and closes every opened reader before returning. Repeated access opens no additional readers.

Rejects POSITION_DELETES and EQUALITY_DELETES entries in the root, identifying their content type and location.

Groups four distinct ADDED, DELETED, MODIFIED, and REPLACED files into their corresponding change collections.

removedVersionsRetainStats
Preserves projected stats on removed and replaced data-file versions for later validation.

colocatedDVsAreNotStandaloneDeleteFiles
Retains a data file's deletion-vector descriptor without reporting standalone delete-file additions or removals.

changesAreLoadedOnce
Any of the six accessors can trigger loading. The input is traversed and closed once; subsequent accesses reuse the results.

failedLoadsAreNotRetried
An iteration failure closes the input and is rethrown by subsequent accessors without another read or close.

The leaf wrapper accepts only data files and writes tracking as given so unassigned sequence numbers and first row IDs are inherited on read, rejecting null sequence numbers that cannot be inherited.

After a partition field is added and then dropped (e.g., when a partition change gets rolled back), the table goes back to its old spec ID. body:
Problem
A spherical geography edge follows a minor great-circle arc. Its latitude can reach a maximum or minimum between the endpoints, so a box built from endpoint coordinates can exclude part of the edge.
For example, the arc from A = (0°, 60°) to B = (90°, 60°), in (longitude, latitude) order, reaches about 67.7923°N at 45°E. Both endpoints are at 60°N. Geography file statistics need to cover the full arc before they can support safe pruning.

The purple box includes outward numerical padding. Its north bound is approximately 67.7923525°N; the padding is too small to see at this scale.
Algorithm
The package-private builder accumulates points and minor great-circle edges into a BoundingBox.

Longitude: Merge the longitude intervals covered by the edges. Longitude is circular, so a box that crosses the antimeridian stores west > east.
Latitude: Convert the endpoints to 3D unit vectors. Their cross product defines the great-circle plane. For a non-equatorial great circle, project the north pole onto that plane and normalize to find the northern latitude extremum; the opposite point gives the southern candidate. Include only candidates on the edge's minor arc, together with the endpoint latitudes.
Numerical handling: Pad accepted extrema outward to guard against rounding. When the cross product is very small, the endpoint dot product distinguishes short arcs from nearly antipodal edges. Short arcs receive conservative latitude padding; unresolved nearly antipodal edges use world bounds.

Coincident endpoints are treated as a point. Pole vertices retain their stored longitude. NaN ordinates do not contribute to their dimension. Empty input or a missing dimension produces no bounds. Out-of-range or infinite coordinates permanently suppress bounds, including after a world-bounds fallback.
Scope
This PR provides the bounds calculation for spherical points and edges. WKB traversal, polygon interior bounds, writer integration, and scan planning are separate work.
Part of #18705. Related spherical bounds implementation: #17788.

Reproduce rounding undercoverage for short arcs and extrema near the equator. Check the near-antipodal fallback boundary.
Check NaN handling, invalid coordinates, empty input, and suppression after invalid input.
Check that sampled points along seeded random minor arcs lie within the returned bounds.

All 89 spherical tests and 16 longitude tests pass on Java 17. Core Spotless and Checkstyle main/test pass.

Summary
Fixes #18758 by preventing a transaction with directly staged metadata from reporting success after a concurrent commit silently discards its changes.
RESTCatalogAdapter.commitTransaction stages changes through CatalogHandlers.commit on transaction TableOperations, without registering a PendingUpdate. After a conflicting commit, BaseTransaction.applyUpdates refreshes the table and replays an empty pending-update list, discarding the intended write and potentially returning success.
Fix
If the table changed and there are no pending updates to replay, fail with a non-retryable CommitFailedException through the existing PendingUpdateFailedException path. Preserve the normal retry/replay behavior when pending updates exist.

Both cases are added to the parameterized TestTransaction suite.

body:
Description
Fixes #18902.
When a REST commit request fails after it has been sent (no response, a connection reset, a read
timeout), HTTPClient wraps the IOException in a plain RESTException. The server may have
applied the commit, but the client reports an ordinary failure: it never raises
CommitStateUnknownException, and RESTTableOperations never tries the reconciliation it already
does for 5xx responses. A caller that retries the failed operation then commits it twice.
This change reports a transport failure on a commit request as CommitStateUnknownException, so it
is handled like a 5xx. Snapshot-add-only commits are reconciled, and other commits are reported as
unknown rather than failed. A ConnectException proves the request was never sent, so it stays a
RESTException. The conversion applies only to commit requests, not to HTTPClient as a whole,
which was the concern raised in #6778.
Changes

Add RESTTableOperations.commitRequest, which converts a RESTException caused by an
IOException (other than ConnectException) into a CommitStateUnknownException.
Use it for table commits in RESTTableOperations.commit, so the existing reconciliation also
covers lost responses.
Use it for multi-table commits in RESTSessionCatalog.commitTransaction.
Add regression tests in TestRESTCatalog:

testReconcileOnLostCommitResponse: the server applies an append but the response is lost; the
commit is reconciled and succeeds.
testLostCommitResponseIsCommitStateUnknown: a lost response to a commit that can't be
reconciled raises CommitStateUnknownException.
testCommitThatCannotConnectIsNotCommitStateUnknown: a ConnectException stays a
RESTException.
testLostTransactionResponseIsCommitStateUnknown: the same for a multi-table transaction.

Validation

Core TestRESTCatalog and TestHTTPClient: passed (257 tests, on main at ab8a86d).
Spotless Java formatting: passed.
git diff --check: passed.
End to end, with Spark 3.5 against apache/iceberg-rest-fixture and a proxy that forwards one
commit and then drops the connection (the reproduction in #18902): with this change applied to
1.12.0, the INSERT reports success and the row is committed once; without it, the INSERT
fails with RESTException although the row was committed.

Notes for reviewers

Any IOException other than ConnectException is treated as a possibly-sent request. Some of
those can happen before the request is sent (for example a TLS handshake failure). Those now
report an unknown state instead of a failure. That is conservative: the engine skips cleanup and
may leave orphan files, but it never deletes files a commit references.
I haven't checked how this interacts with the HTTP client's own retry strategy. In the end-to-end
run, the commit request reached the catalog only once.
The end-to-end check used a Spark runtime built from 1.12.0 with this change, not one built from
main.

Closes #18901
SparkBatch.planInputPartitions() broadcasts the table and the FileIO on every call, and SparkScan.toBatch() returns a new SparkBatch each time. Spark plans input partitions for every copy of a scan node, during planning. When dynamic partition pruning filters nest over a chain of joins on a partition column, the number of copies is exponential and each leaves two broadcasts in the driver until the plan is released. A production query with 10 such joins created 264,382 broadcasts and exhausted driver memory before starting a stage. This PR creates the broadcasts once per scan and shares them between its batches. It does not change how many subqueries Spark plans.
Backports to Spark 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1 will follow once this change is merged.
Test plan (TestScanBroadcastReuse):

Planning input partitions again for the same scan creates no new broadcasts. This is the behavior the change adds.
A six-way left join on the partition column with DPP enabled stays below the number of nested filters (2^6). This checks that Spark shares one scan between the plan copies, which the fix depends on. Without the change the query creates more than 400 broadcasts.

body: AuthSession.fromTokenResponse() and refresh() set the session's expiresAtMillis only from the exp claim of a JWT access token; expires_in from the token response was used to schedule the background refresh but never stored on the session. With authorization servers that issue opaque (non-JWT) access tokens, AuthSession.expiresAtMillis() is therefore always null, so the expired-token branches in refreshCurrentToken() and fromAccessToken() never engage. This falls back to startTime + expires_in when the token is not a JWT (RFC 6749 §5.1), in both places. testCatalogTokenRefreshFailsAndUsesCredentialForRefresh drops from two token-exchange attempts to one: with the expiry known, the retry sees the 1 s token as expired and goes straight to the credential flow, as that branch intends.

This PR supersedes #17901 by @fmorillo7694. It keeps their original commit, rebases it onto main, and addresses the open review comment. All credit for the fix and the regression test goes to them. If they'd rather continue in #17901, I'm happy to close this PR.
Problem
IcebergCommitter reads getMaxCommittedCheckpointId() once, before the commit. Another commit for the same checkpoint can land after that read, and the second commit then applies cleanly on top of the first. The checkpoint's files are committed twice. See #17901 and #14425 for the original analysis and the deterministic reproduction.
We also hit this in production with blue/green deployments, where the old job keeps running for a short time after the savepoint is taken. The old job commits checkpoint N. Seconds later, the new job commits the same committable, which it restored from the savepoint, under the same job ID. In one table, we found 10 data files that were each added twice, in consecutive snapshots.
Changes
The first commit is the original change from #17901, rebased onto main. The second commit makes these changes:

Moves MaxCommittedCheckpointIdValidator into SinkUtil, as @mxm asked in #17901 (comment). Its mismatch exception moves with it.
Adapts the validator to #18303. DynamicCommitter now identifies its own snapshots by sink ID, and IcebergCommitter still uses the job ID and operator ID. So each caller now passes a predicate that matches its own snapshot summaries.
In IcebergCommitter, validates only after a restore. This matches the up-front check since #18123. After a stateless start, a job can reuse its job ID while its checkpoint IDs start from 1 again. Without this condition, the validator would skip those commits and silently drop data. testCommitTxnAfterStatelessRestart caught this. Duplicate commits come from restored committables, so restored jobs, including blue/green deployments, are still protected.
Updates the regression test for the new IcebergCommitter constructor.

Like #17901, this targets Flink 2.3 only. Backports can follow once the approach is approved.
Testing

TestIcebergCommitterDuplicateCommit passes. It fails when the validator is disabled, with 2 snapshots instead of 1.
TestIcebergCommitter (336), TestIcebergFilesCommitter (96), TestIcebergSink (312), TestDynamicCommitter (14) and TestDynamicIcebergSink (50) all pass.
spotlessCheck, checkstyleMain and checkstyleTest pass.

Truncate cuts strings to a width in code points, but the startsWith and notStartsWith projections compared the prefix's UTF-16 length with that width. SortOrder#satisfies compares the two orders field by field with SortField#satisfies. That allows a finer transform to stand in for a coarser one, such as ts for day(ts). This is only valid for the last field of the order being satisfied.
When another field follows, rows that tie on the coarse value must still be ordered by the next field. Sorting by [ts, symbol] orders the rows within a day by ts first. symbol is not ordered within the day, so the data is not sorted by [day(ts), symbol]. Before this change, [ts, symbol].satisfies([day(ts), symbol]) returned true.
This change requires every field of the other order except the last to match exactly (equals). Only the last field may be satisfied by a finer transform:

this
other
before
after

[ts]
[day(ts)]
true
true

[symbol, ts]
[symbol, day(ts)]
true
true

[ts, symbol]
[day(ts), symbol]
true
false

Impact: SortOrder#satisfies is public API and nothing in this repo calls it from main code. An engine that uses it to decide whether existing data is already sorted could skip a needed sort and write wrongly ordered output. Callers affected by this change will now do the sort they previously skipped. SortOrderUtil calls Transform#satisfiesOrderOf directly, stops after the first non-matching field, and is unaffected.
Tests: added TestSortOrder#testSatisfiesTransformFollowedByAnotherField.
AI disclosure: AI assistance was used in this PR. I reviewed the logic and ran TestSortOrder.
title: API: Fix SortOrder#satisfies for transforms followed by other fields

Backport of #11731 to 1.6.x, as done for 1.7.x in 5a4e4e2 (released in 1.7.2).
Fixes #18927
Why
Since Spark 3.5.4 (SPARK-50235, SPARK-50463), the generated ColumnarToRow code calls closeIfFreeable() after each batch. IcebergArrowColumnVector reuses its Arrow vectors across batches but does not override it, so with Iceberg 1.6.x on Spark 3.5.4+, every row after the first vectorized batch of a data file is read from released buffers: wrong values without an error, or executor crashes. Details and a reproduction in #18927.
1.6.1 is the last release that supports Java 8, so Java 8 users of Spark 3.5 cannot get the fix by upgrading to 1.7.2.
Changes
Same as #11731 (cherry-picked from 5a4e4e2):

IcebergArrowColumnVector: empty closeIfFreeable() override.
spark-hive35: 3.5.1 → 3.5.4, so the Spark 3.5 module is built and tested against a version that calls closeIfFreeable(). The other version bumps of #11731 do not apply to 1.6.x.

Testing

Built the Spark 3.5 runtime jar with Java 8.
With the reproduction from #18927 (Spark 3.5.8, one 1,000-row file, batch size 100): 0 wrong rows with this branch, 900 with the 1.6.1 jar.

body:
This PR improves file pruning for IN predicates on columns that use non-order-preserving partition transforms such as bucket.
Partition projection already limits a manifest scan to matching bucket values. File metrics evaluation, however, still evaluates every literal in the original IN predicate against every selected file. A literal assigned to another bucket can therefore retain a file that cannot contain that literal. Lists above the metrics evaluator's 200-value limit also skip bounds evaluation before literals are narrowed to the file's partition.
The change binds the row filter once and pre-indexes eligible IN literals by transformed partition value. For each file, metrics evaluation uses only literals compatible with that file's partition. Existing schema-only InclusiveMetricsEvaluator constructors retain their current behavior. ManifestReader opts into the partition-aware path through InclusiveMetricsEvaluator.forRowFilter.
Validation
./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-api:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.expressions.TestInclusiveMetricsEvaluator
./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-core:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.TestManifestReader
./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-api:spotlessJavaCheck :iceberg-core:spotlessJavaCheck
git diff --check

TestManifestReader covers format versions 1 through 4. It verifies ordinary and 250-value IN predicates, rejects an impossible cross-bucket file, and retains a file that can match.
A synthetic JMH benchmark uses 1,000 buckets, 10,000 files, and broad or narrow file bounds. Deterministic file counts and one-fork timing results are below.
Keys	Layout	Baseline files	Patched files	Baseline ms/op	Patched ms/op
50	narrow	487	50	15.94	16.41
200	narrow	1,815	199	18.61	17.05
400	narrow	3,250	397	17.32	17.32
400	broad	3,250	3,250	17.07	17.91
The timing confidence intervals overlap in every case. In the 400-key narrow case, allocation fell from 13.35 MB/op to 11.21 MB/op. The broad case measures the indexing cost when file counts cannot improve.

title: Improve metrics pruning for bucketed IN predicates
